extracted.intended_audience: organ procurement organizations (OPOs), transplant hospital and provider finance/compliance officers, Medicare contractors, auditors, and policy stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of proposed regulatory criteria on what provider and OPO costs are allowable or unallowable for Medicare reimbursement (prudent buyer rules, entertainment, public education, professional education, travel, and related exclusions). Targeted at OPOs and Medicare providers preparing cost reports or responding to audits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicare reasonable cost principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments for organ procurement and other provider costs under Medicare must not exceed the costs incurred and must be determined in accordance with section 1861(v) of the Act and the regulations in part 413. Costs paid by transplant hospitals (THs) and passed on to Medicare are governed by these statutory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs must be related to patient care, reasonable and necessary, and adequately documented. OPOs seeking Medicare payment must enter into an agreement with CMS. CMS proposes to apply Medicare's reasonable cost principles and the part 413 regulations to OPOs and HCLs; amounts not meeting these requirements may be disallowed (OIG audits identified unallowable costs when providers misunderstood these principles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudent buyer principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A provider is expected to economize and not pay more than a prudent and cost-conscious buyer would pay for an item or service; the provider should seek discounts, warranties, and other cost savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If costs exceed what prudent buyers incur, excess costs are not reimbursable absent clear evidence they were unavoidable. PRM examples of noncompliance include consistently buying from a higher-priced supplier without justification, failing to reflect indirect discounts (e.g., rental as discount), leasing equipment from a staff physician when competitive bids would be cheaper, and failing to obtain warranty credits. Methods contractors may use to detect excessive costs include comparing prices with comparable purchasers, spot-checking, querying providers, using IRS Form 990 to compare compensation, using federal per diem rates for accommodations, examining provider records, and considering geographic variations. Joint purchasing arrangements may require non-participating providers to justify higher prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unallowable entertainment costs (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs incurred by providers for entertainment are not allowable for Medicare reimbursement because they are not reasonable costs related to patient care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS proposes to codify that entertainment costs are unallowable and to specify examples (proposed §413.5(c)(10) and (c)(10)(i)). Examples include tickets/admission to sporting or other events, sponsorship of sporting events/teams/athletes (including motorsports), sponsorship of floats in national parades, concerts/theater/performing arts/professional musicians, wine tours/alcoholic beverages, retreats at spas or luxury resorts, golf outings, ski trips, cruises, and similar recreational excursions. OIG audit findings (e.g., Rose Parade, race car sponsorships) are cited as examples of unallowable entertainment expenses reported as public education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable OPO public education costs (community-based, targeted outreach)
rubrics_metrics.description: OPO public education costs are allowable only when they are reasonable, necessary, related to patient care, and constitute direct, community-based, locally focused outreach within the OPO's donation service area (DSA) that facilitates one-on-one engagement and donor registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowable activities include booths at local farmer's markets, health fairs, high school/college sporting events, partnering with community/faith groups, local multicultural festivals, driver's education programs, and DMV or similar offices where individuals can register. OPOs should track number of registrations during each effort, have staff available to answer questions, and may provide modest tokens and educational materials (pens, bracelets, buttons, cups, web/QR info). Such initiatives must not violate the entertainment-costs prohibition and must be measurable and targeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: National-level public awareness/outreach by OPOs (not allowable)
rubrics_metrics.description: OPOs should not seek Medicare reimbursement for national organ donor awareness campaigns or national-level outreach activities that are duplicative of HRSA's public awareness efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HRSA is authorized to develop and partner on national public awareness programs and historically has funded and continues ongoing national outreach (Organdonor.gov, PSAs, paid media, billboards, etc.). Medicare reimbursement for similar national-level activities by individual OPOs may be duplicative and therefore inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee and non-employee entertainment costs (disallowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs for employee or non-employee entertainment activities and employee morale events are not allowable costs under Medicare because they are not related to patient care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS proposes to change PRM policy to disallow such costs (proposed §413.5(c)(12)), including but not limited to picnics, parties, performers, entertainment, award ceremonies, sponsorship of scholarships or athletic programs. CMS notes alternative, cost-effective morale methods (flexible schedules, wellness programs) and distinguishes these from allowable fringe benefits that are part of formal written policies (e.g., health insurance, retirement plans) which may be allowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcoholic beverages costs (disallowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: A provider's costs to furnish alcoholic beverages to anyone are not allowable costs for Medicare reimbursement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS proposes to codify this longstanding PRM policy (proposed §413.5(c)(13)). PRM language and OIG audits document instances where providers included costs for furnishing alcohol on cost reports; such costs are unrelated to patient care and not appropriate for reimbursement.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPO professional education costs (non-CE seminars for clinical staff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs for OPO-sponsored meetings, seminars, and presentations that do not provide continuing education (CE) credits are allowable when the content is directly related to organ donation and the acquisition of all usable organs and the attendees are clinical staff (OPO personnel, donor hospital staff, physicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed §413.5(c)(14)(i) codifies this: such costs must meet Medicare reasonable cost principles (related to patient care, reasonable, necessary). This codifies and clarifies prior statements that non-CE seminars can be allowable if patient-care related.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPO professional education costs (CE seminars — OPO staff vs. non-OPO staff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs for OPO-sponsored seminars that provide CE credits are allowable only when the attendees are OPO staff; costs are not allowable when CE seminars' attendees are not OPO staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS proposes §413.5(c)(14)(ii) to allow CE seminar costs limited to OPO staff to the extent patient-care related, reasonable and necessary; and §413.5(c)(14)(iii) (and cross-references to §413.402) to disallow CE seminar costs when attendees are not OPO staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff training, orientation, and employee education costs (allowable when patient-care related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs of staff training and education (including orientation and on-the-job training) are allowable provided they are reasonable and related to patient care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRM-1 sections cited: orientation and on-the-job training recognized as normal operating expenses; outside instruction costs may be allowable; items provided for the convenience of the provider (provider-paid educational courses, uniforms, operating day care centers) may be includable to the extent reasonable and related to patient care. Continuous safety and training programs aimed at reducing malpractice/workers' comp incidents are required and recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel costs for professional education (allowability limits and minimization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel costs incurred for employee attendance at professional education are generally allowable when patient-care related and reasonable; foreign travel requires clear substantiation; overnight travel allowable under specified conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRM guidance: local travel generally allowable; foreign travel allowable only when provider substantiates reasonableness and patient-care relatedness. CMS proposes overnight travel costs are allowable when the event is >50 miles from workplace and requires >8 hours of attendance (reflecting standard business practices). Providers expected to minimize travel costs by selecting economy/coach accommodations. Costs for personal use of provider vehicles are unallowable. Education expenses for spouses or other dependents are unallowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs for drugs sold to others (disallowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs incurred by providers for drugs sold to other than patients are not related to patient care and are not allowable costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS proposes to codify PRM-1 chapter 21 policy by adding §413.5(c)(17) specifying this exclusion (costs of drugs sold to others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs for fines or penalties (disallowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs incurred by providers for fines or penalties resulting from Federal, State, or local laws are not allowable costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS proposes to codify this longstanding PRM policy by adding §413.5(c)(18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs to operate a gift shop (disallowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs incurred by providers for the operation of a gift shop are not allowable costs because they are not related to patient care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS proposes to codify the PRM-1 policy by adding §413.5(c)(19) to make this explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirement: OPO contractual agreement and payment flow
rubrics_metrics.description: An OPO must enter into an agreement with CMS to seek Medicare payment for organ procurement costs; transplant hospitals bill Medicare for transplant and organ acquisition costs, and costs paid by THs and passed to Medicare are governed by the Medicare statute and regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains the billing flow and why OPOs' costs are governed by Medicare reasonable cost principles — OPOs' organ acquisition costs provided to THs (and paid by THs) fall under section 1861(v) and part 413, so OPOs must comply with applicable Medicare payment rules and documentation requirements.
